steps.title: Titles, Axis Labels, and Legends
steps.lede: A chart without labels forces the reader to guess — three method calls make it self-explanatory.

blocks.text: Titles, axis labels, and legends are the text that tells a reader what a plot shows. Matplotlib gives two parallel ways to add them, depending on whether you are working with an Axes object or the pyplot interface directly.

`ax.set_xlabel('...')` and `ax.set_ylabel('...')` set the x-axis and y-axis labels, and `ax.set_title('...')` sets the Axes title. `ax.set_xlabel('Day')`, `ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)')`, and `ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day')` label the Lagos trend line.

Passing `label='...'` to a plotting call and then calling `ax.legend()` displays a legend identifying each labeled series. `ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label='Lagos')` followed by `ax.legend()` shows a legend identifying the Lagos line — which matters once a second city's line is added.

annotations.text: No labels — the reader cannot tell what the axes or line represent

after.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label='Lagos')
ax.set_xlabel('Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)')
ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day')
ax.legend()

annotations.text: label='Lagos' names this series for the legend
ax.legend() displays the legend for all labeled series

tiles.title: Seaborn: DataFrame Plotting, Statistical Functions, and Themes
tiles.summary: Use seaborn's dataframe-aware plotting functions, add automatic statistical estimates with sns.regplot(), and apply themes and palettes with sns.set_theme().

steps.title: Plotting Directly from a DataFrame with Seaborn
steps.lede: Seaborn's functions take column names instead of extracted arrays — less code, same chart.

blocks.text: Most matplotlib calls so far have needed you to pull a column out of `orders` yourself before plotting it. Seaborn's plotting functions operate on dataframes and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot (for example `data=`, `x=`, `y=`) rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

`seaborn.barplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` visualizes an aggregate statistical estimate for each category as a bar; its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar by default. `sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes')` produces a per-city mean bar chart without a groupby call.

blocks.title: Average Delivery Time by City — seaborn barplot

steps.title: Automatic Statistical Estimates with Seaborn
steps.lede: Many seaborn functions compute a statistical estimate for you — sns.regplot() adds a fitted regression line to a scatter plot.

blocks.text: Many seaborn functions will automatically perform the statistical estimation necessary to answer questions such as the average value of one variable as a function of other variables. `sns.barplot()` already does this — it computes the mean per category without a groupby call.

`seaborn.regplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` plots a scatterplot of the observations together with a fitted linear regression line. `sns.regplot(data=orders, x='distance_km', y='delivery_time_minutes')` draws each order as a point and overlays the best-fit line through those points.

steps.title: Applying Themes and Palettes with sns.set_theme()
steps.lede: One call before your plot changes the background, gridlines, and colors for every chart that follows.

blocks.text: `seaborn.set_theme()` accepts a `style` parameter (default `'darkgrid'`) and a `palette` parameter (default `'deep'`) among its arguments, which set the plot's background/gridline style and its color palette respectively. `sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')` switches to a white background with gridlines.

`sns.set_theme(style=..., palette=...)` changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn. Calling `sns.set_theme()` changes how plots drawn after that call look — it does not restyle a figure you already drew and displayed.

steps.title: Style Sheets, rcParams, and Seaborn Palettes
steps.lede: Three tools let you control the visual appearance of every chart: style sheets, rcParams, and seaborn palettes.

blocks.text: `plt.style.use('style-name')` applies one of matplotlib's predefined style sheets — for example `'ggplot'` or `'dark_background'`. The available styles can be listed with `plt.style.available`.

A custom style file can set specific properties such as `'axes.titlesize'`, `'lines.linewidth'`, or tick label sizes, and rcParams can be set directly to change defaults globally. After `import matplotlib as mpl`, `mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2` sets the default line width for every plot drawn after that call.

`seaborn.set_palette(palette, ...)` sets the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette, applying that color scheme to subsequent plots. `sns.set_palette('pastel')` switches later plots to seaborn's pastel color scheme.

before.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg)

annotations.text: Default matplotlib style — grey background, thin lines

after.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
plt.style.use('ggplot')
mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg)

mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2 sets the default line width globally

steps.title: Arranging Multiple Charts in One Figure
steps.lede: plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a grid of Axes — each panel is independent.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to show the delivery-time histogram and the distance/delivery-time scatter plot together, side by side, instead of as two separate figures.

`fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` creates a Figure containing a grid of Axes with the given number of rows and columns. `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` creates one Figure holding four Axes arranged in two rows and two columns.

Each Axes in the returned grid is indexed separately (for example `axs[0, 0]`) and plotting/labeling calls made on one Axes only affect that panel. `axs[0, 0].hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` draws the histogram into the top-left panel, and `axs[0, 1].scatter(orders['distance_km'], orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` draws the scatter into the top-right panel without disturbing the first.

blocks.alt_text: A 2×2 grid of panels inside one Figure. Each panel is labelled with its Axes index (axs[0,0] through axs[1,1]) and a chart type. Plotting on one panel does not affect the others.

steps.title: Making charts readable with labels
steps.lede: A chart without labels is just shapes. Three Axes methods and one legend call fix that.

blocks.text: Titles, axis labels, and legends are the text that tells a reader what a plot shows. Matplotlib gives two parallel ways to add them: the Axes object interface and the pyplot interface. On an Axes object, ax.set_xlabel('Day'), ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)'), and ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day') label the Lagos trend line.

When you plot multiple series on the same Axes, a legend shows which line is which. Pass label='Lagos' to ax.plot(), then call ax.legend(). Once a second city's line is added to the same Axes, the legend identifies each series by its label.

before.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg)
plt.show()
# No title, no axis labels, no legend

annotations.text: Plot draws, but the reader has no context

after.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]
ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label='Lagos')
ax.set_xlabel('Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Average delivery time (minutes)')
ax.set_title('Average delivery time by day')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

steps.title: Choosing the right chart for your question
steps.lede: Five chart types, five different questions. The chart you pick changes what the reader sees.

blocks.text: With five chart types available, the question during exploration is which one actually answers the question you're asking of the data. Picking a chart type comes down to naming what you're asking: a category comparison, a single variable's spread, a trend over time, a relationship between two variables, or a spread comparison across several groups.

A bar chart compares values across categories—average delivery time per city. plt.hist() bins a numeric variable and draws its distribution—how delivery times are spread out. Line graphs show how a value changes over time—average delivery time across days of the week. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables—whether distance and delivery time move together. Boxplots compare the distributions of multiple datasets side by side—the full spread of delivery times across several cities at once.

blocks.text: plt.style.use('ggplot') changes the look of all plots drawn after that call—background color, grid lines, font sizes, and more. You can see all available style names by printing plt.style.available. Call it once at the top of your notebook to set a consistent look.

remediation_steps.title: Let's review
remediation_steps.lede: Here's another way to think about subplot indexing.

blocks.text: When plt.subplots(2, 2) returns axs, think of it as a 2D grid. axs[0, 0] is the top-left panel, axs[0, 1] is top-right, axs[1, 0] is bottom-left, axs[1, 1] is bottom-right. Plotting on axs[0, 0] only affects that one panel—the others stay empty until you plot on them.

steps.eyebrow: Plotting directly from pandas DataFrames with seaborn
steps.title: seaborn's DataFrame-first interface
steps.lede: seaborn functions take a DataFrame and column names—no array extraction needed.

blocks.text: Most matplotlib calls require you to extract a column from orders yourself before plotting it. Seaborn's plotting functions operate on DataFrames and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot—data=, x=, y=—rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes') plots average delivery time per city directly from the orders DataFrame and its column names—no separate .groupby() call needed first. Its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar automatically.

steps.title: Automatic statistical estimation
steps.lede: Some seaborn functions compute statistics—means, regression lines—automatically.

blocks.text: Many seaborn functions automatically perform the statistical estimation necessary to answer questions such as the average value of one variable as a function of other variables. The sns.barplot() call from before is one such example—it computed each city's mean delivery time automatically, without a separate .groupby() step.

sns.regplot(data=orders, x='distance_km', y='delivery_time_minutes') plots a scatterplot of the observations together with a fitted linear regression line. It shows the distance/delivery-time scatter with a fitted trend line drawn through it in the same call—no separate fitting step required.

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.regplot(data=orders, x='distance_km', y='delivery_time_minutes')
plt.show()

steps.eyebrow: seaborn built-in themes and color palettes
steps.title: Polishing plots with sns.set_theme()
steps.lede: sns.set_theme() changes the global defaults for all plots—seaborn and matplotlib alike.

blocks.text: sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep') switches to a white background with gridlines and seaborn's 'deep' color palette. The style parameter (default 'darkgrid') controls the background and gridlines; the palette parameter (default 'deep') controls the color sequence.

sns.set_theme() changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn. Because it works by changing global defaults, calling sns.set_theme() changes how plots drawn after that call look—it does not restyle a figure already displayed.

before.title: Default matplotlib style
before.alt_text: Bar chart of category vs value using ds.theming_demo with matplotlib's default white background, blue bars, and no gridlines.

after.code:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')
sns.barplot(data=theming_demo, x='category', y='value')
plt.show()
# White background, gridlines, seaborn 'deep' palette

annotations.text: set_theme applies style and palette globally via rcParams

remediation_steps.title: Let's review
remediation_steps.lede: Here's another way to think about seaborn's DataFrame interface.

blocks.text: With matplotlib you write city_avg = orders.groupby('city')['delivery_time_minutes'].mean() then ax.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg.values). With seaborn you write sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes'). The difference: seaborn takes the whole DataFrame and column names as strings, computing the mean automatically.

remediation_steps.title: Let's review
remediation_steps.lede: Here's another way to think about seaborn's automatic estimation.

blocks.text: When you call sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes'), seaborn computes the mean delivery time for each city automatically—you don't need a .groupby().mean() step first. This automatic statistical estimation is what makes seaborn different from matplotlib's raw plotting functions.
